sections.title: Verb + object + to-infinitive
sections.content:
After some verbs we need to include an object before a to-infinitive in active sentences:
• The police warned everyone to stay inside with their windows closed. (not The police warned to stay ...)
Also: advise, allow, believe, cause, command, enable, encourage, entitle, force, invite, order, persuade, remind, teach, tell
After other verbs, however, we can't include an object before a to-infinitive:
• We've decided to leave early. (not We've decided us to leave early.)
Also: agree, consent, fail, hope, manage, offer, pretend, refuse, start, threaten, volunteer

sections.title: Prepositions with object + to-infinitive
sections.content:
After some verbs we have to put a preposition, usually for, between the verb and the object + to-infinitive:
• They arranged for Rania to stay in London. (not They arranged Rania to stay ...)
• They applied for the court appearance to be postponed.
Also: advertise, campaign, long, plan, wait
Other verbs can be followed by different prepositions + object + to-infinitive:
• at + object + to-infinitive (go on, keep on, scream, shout, yell): I shouted at the man to open the door.
• on + object + to-infinitive (call, count, depend, prevail, rely): We're depending on you to find a solution soon.
• to + object + to-infinitive (appeal, gesture, motion, signal): He closed the door and signalled to the pilot to take off.

sections.title: Negative forms and other patterns
sections.content:
A number of other to-infinitive and -ing forms can also follow verbs:
• verb + negative to-infinitive/negative -ing: We decided not to go to Paris after all. / Some of my friends have considered not going to college.
• verb + to have + past participle: The accident seems to have happened at around 1 pm yesterday. (Often used to give an opinion or report what is said about a past event).
• verb + having + past participle: I now regret buying the car. or I now regret having bought the car. (Often used with admit, deny, forget, recall, regret, remember).

exercises.question: My mother ___ me to throw away my old toys.
exercises.hint: Threatened doesn't take an object before the infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: told
Threatened doesn't take an object before the infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.sentence: He agreed taking the position despite the long commute involved.
exercises.correction: He agreed to take the position despite the long commute involved.
exercises.hint: 'Agree' is followed by a to-infinitive, not a gerund.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: agreed to take
'Agree' is followed by a to-infinitive: agree to do. Other verbs that take only a to-infinitive: decide, expect, hope, intend, manage, offer, plan, prepare, promise, refuse, tend, want, wish. A useful test: if the action follows a conscious decision or intention, it usually takes a to-infinitive.

exercises.question: My mother ___ to throw away my old toys.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: threatened
'Tell' always requires a direct object (a person told): 'tell someone to do something', 'tell someone that...'. Compare 'say', which does not need an object person.

exercises.sentence: They decided going by train rather than driving for the whole journey.
exercises.correction: They decided to go by train rather than driving for the whole journey.
exercises.hint: 'Decide' takes a to-infinitive: decide to do.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: decided to go
'Decide' is always followed by 'to + infinitive'. It expresses a conscious, deliberate choice. The gerund after 'decide' is not standard: you cannot say 'decide doing'. Note: 'decided on going' is possible but uses a different pattern (decide on + gerund).

exercises.question: When I advertised ___ a website designer...
exercises.explanation:
Answer: for
The preposition after 'advertise' when seeking someone or something is 'for': 'advertise for a job', 'advertise for a flatmate'. 'Advertise' without 'for' means to promote or publicise.

exercises.question: After three rounds of negotiation, they finally managed ___ (reach) an agreement.
exercises.hint: 'Manage' takes a to-infinitive and implies effort or difficulty.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: to reach
'Manage' is always followed by a to-infinitive and implies that achieving the result required effort or was not easy: 'manage to do' = succeed in doing despite difficulty. Compare: 'could do' (general ability) vs 'managed to do' (specific achievement after effort).

exercises.question: But I've now learnt that you can't rely ___ Greta to do anything.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: on
The preposition after 'rely' is always 'on': 'rely on someone'. This is a fixed collocation. Compare: 'depend on', 'count on', 'trust' (no preposition).

exercises.question: I ___ anyone Marta's new address. (agree - not tell)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: agreed not to tell
Agree + not + to-infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: The prisoners ___ through a broken window last night. (think - escape)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are thought to have escaped
News reports and announcements use the present perfect to introduce a recent event with current relevance. The exact time is less important than the fact that the event has just happened and affects the present situation. After the first mention, the past simple is used for the details.
